chunks: From him, from Ubayd Allah ibn al-Fadl ibn Muhammad ibn Hilal, from Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath al-Kinani, who said: Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us from his father, who said: My father narrated to me from his father from his grandfather from Ali (peace be upon him), who said:

Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) used to say: 'The testimony of women is not valid in hudud (fixed punishments) and qawd (retaliation).' As for what these two reports encompass, it is possible that the intended meaning is that their testimony is not accepted in hudud except for rajm (stoning), because we have not established the testimony of women in the punishment of theft and drinking wine, and what runs in its manner among the hudud, and we have restricted it to rajm and the punishment of zina (fornication).

As for what the report of Ibrahim al-Kharraqi, and the report of Zurara, and Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, and Abu Basir, encompassed, which is that the testimony of women is not accepted in blood (diyah/retaliation).

(711) 116 What does not contradict this is what was narrated - Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Jamil ibn Darraj and Ibn Humran from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: We said: Is the testimony of women valid in hudud? He said: 'In killing alone, indeed Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: 'The blood of a Muslim man is not nullified'.'

Because the way to reconcile between these reports is that their testimony is not accepted in blood when qawd (retaliation) is established by their testimony, although it is permissible to accept it in establishing diyah (blood money), and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) drew attention to this by his saying: Indeed Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: 'The blood of a Muslim man is not nullified'.

And the two reports we mentioned from Ghiyath ibn Ibrahim and Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Ash'ath also confirm this, because what is negated by their testimony in them is qawd, not diyah, and it is possible that the meaning is that their testimony is not accepted in blood if there are not men with them, and it is accepted with the presence of men with them.

(712) 117 And that which reveals what we mentioned is what was narrated - Yunus ibn Abd al-Rahman from al-Mufaddal ibn Salih from Zayd al-Shahham, who said: I asked him about the testimony of women, so he said: 'The testimony of women is not valid in rajm except with three men and two women, so if there are two men and four women, it is not valid in rajm.' He said: I said: Is the testimony of women valid with men in blood (diyah)? He said: 'Yes'.
ai.seo_question: Is the testimony of women valid in Islamic criminal punishments and blood money?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi synthesizes conflicting reports to establish a nuanced Shia jurisprudence where women's testimony is excluded from fixed punishments (hudud) like stoning and retaliation (qawd) unless accompanied by men, yet remains valid for establishing blood money (diyah). This distinction is rooted in the principle that 'the blood of a Muslim is not invalidated,' ensuring that financial compensation is secured even if the stricter evidentiary requirements for corporal punishment are not met. The text highlights the scholarly effort to reconcile the general prohibition with specific exceptions, emphasizing the protective nature of the law regarding the preservation of life and property.
